content.title: ‘DTF St. Louis’ Recap, Season 1 Episode 5: ‘Amphezyne’
content.text: DTF St. Louis Recap: Time Alone From the World Amphezyne Season 1 Episode 5 Editor’s Rating 3 stars DTF St. Louis Amphezyne Season 1 Episode 5 Editor’s Rating 3 stars Floyd, Clark, and Carol’s love triangle takes a turn for the strange, but it doesn’t feel all that deadly. Photo: Tina Rowden/HBO Dubious as I’ve been (and remain) of the show’s thin mystery structure, “Amphezyne” steadies the ship for the remainder of the journey by moving the mystery part sufficiently out of the way of the absurd suburban theater at its twisted, tender core. “It isn’t really the sex,” Floyd tells Clark at the gym, having just revealed he knows about Clark and Carol’s affair. “What you really share is time alone from the world.” Just past the halfway mark of its seven-episode run, DTF St. Louis takes us to the emotional and physical core of Floyd, Clark, and Carol’s love triangle. After multiple teases of this pivotal confrontational moment, we finally get the full breadth of the conversation. Floyd asks for an invite to the next Quality Gardens outing to watch Carol and Clark from the closet. Again, the kink here — “Can I watch?” — is pretty pedestrian, but Floyd’s emotional motivations are already clear to him to the point of being nigh on heartbreaking. Both he and Carol, having lost their “time alone from the world” with each other, have found it in Clark’s arms. Now Floyd wants to reclaim a slice of that lost intimacy with Carol, through the intimacy they’ve found separately in Clark. This is also where the viewer will likely find their assumptions or hypotheses about Floyd’s death and the guilty party (or parties) involved start sifting through their fingers like sand. As audience proxy, Detective Homer says as much in a late-night heart-to-heart with Plumb. “I thought this case was gonna be open-and-shut because it’s the suburbs. It’s regular people. It’s normal.” But the genuine love for Floyd that the detectives have gleaned from both Clark and Carol continues to move the case away from a “normal” Lifetime Original movie–style marital infidelity–to–murder pipeline. I’m still dubious of the form of this story’s mystery structure, but we are getting closer to a sense of genuine narrative function here. Even when people are doing shameful things or committing crimes, the web of traumas and emotional blows that lead up to them is seldom, if ever, the cut-and-dried story you tell yourself at first glance. Case in point: Turns out that Amphezyne subscription was Floyd’s idea. The request comes sometime after their first Quality Gardens encounter as a trio (or threesome, if you prefer). Floyd seems interested enough in the scene from the closet (as evidenced by naming aloud the rimjob request Clark is spelling on Carol’s back — hilarious setup, economically executed with an understated panache) but can’t help ditching the play to save a deaf and blind kid from walking into the pool outside. Clark and Carol look on, a mixture of awe and exhaustion, as Floyd signs with this kid through his hands during another comically sappy pep talk. Floyd feels good when his heart is wide open to the whole world, making him a Good Samaritan and his own type of lousy partner all at once. Love Carol though he does, he can’t focus on her and really see her in the moment. Meet her where she’s at. Later on, during a weird nighttime parking-lot heart-to-heart, Floyd asks Clark to help him get his hands on some Amphezyne to help his broken boner work better. But his physical malady is only half his problem. Cue another chapter in the Peyronie’s origin story, multiple red herrings in which Floyd injures himself practically everywhere but his penis, and no conclusion in sight. Listen, I know this running gag of the never-ending broken-dick origin story can last only two more episodes, but it’s getting pretty tiresome. Like, finish the story at this point or wait until you’re going to finish it to drop the rest, you know? But if it adds anything to this scene, it’s that Floyd and Carol’s intimacy issues are rooted in a lost ability to be present as a couple. So Clark, for whom physical intimacy with Carol is still something of a new adventure, recommends looking out for those little indescribable, unique physical details of a person that enhance presence and attraction. Like putting your readers on to make words clear again. Jason Bateman delivers the mundane analogy like a pro, blending sincerity and uncertainty inside his singular, nervous vocal rhythms. It’s good advice, too. But will it be enough, even with pharmaceutical assistance? Sometime after the relief of having his life insurance settled, Floyd and Clark propose a new scenario to Carol: Clark watches from the closet at the Quality Gardens while Floyd and Carol act out some “dreams” of their own. “If Clark can be there with you and me in the old ways, and I can be full on [emphasized by impromptu signing gesture that could only mean that kind of full on], and Clark can experience that, then it can be like we were all sharing the experience this summer.” Floyd, as always, seems exhaustingly genuine when he also says he doesn’t want Clark to feel bad about cucking him, and that switching pole (or, in this case, closet) position will bridge the gap in their connecting line of the love triangle. The scene plays like a parody of a therapy video modeling good communication in a marriage or something — a darkly comic reminder that this bubble of therapy-speak-induced denial is doomed to burst. Back in the present time, Plumb and Homer remain suspicious of Carol. After interviewing her together at the top of the episode (where Homer is introduced to her various evasion tactics, including incessant uses of “Can you speak up?” and “No way, José”), they walk away with little to go on except the fact that she evaded the question of prior felonies or convictions, complete with instant recall of the exact code number that says felons with expunged records aren’t obligated to talk. Between Greek-chorusing via investigative dialogue, Homer tries to figure out where Clark’s second recumbent bike went, hoping it’ll lead them to whoever is in the surveillance footage riding up to the pool house. Whaddayaknow, they find it at Carol’s after securing a warrant to search her garage. “Was she capable of murdering her husband for money?” Homer wonders. The episode closes out on Plumb going through with his shady plan: Apply for a job in their department with Carol’s name and info, and they’ll get a rundown of Carol’s prior conviction via background check. With Carol’s guilt still in question and her emotional core still tucked behind the present-day mystery, one can’t help but feel she’s getting the short end of the narrative stick. Whether or not Carol is a murderer or something else. Whether or not she’s capable should be less vague as we inch closer to the final reveal. Still, her motivation both before and after Clark’s death is once again broadcast via a Life Champions audiobook snippet: “Congratulations, you are now equipped to make a comprehensive assessment of where the value is in your surroundings. Go out and identify the dead weight in your life. Cut yourself free from it. Protect yourself and thrive. Now plan, execute, master the conditions of your life.” DTF St. Louis Amphezyne Season 1 Episode 5 Editor’s Rating 3 stars DTF St. Louis Recap: Time Alone From the World Your product is saved!
